bodies:
Add a dedicated ".ipe" keyring for IPE policy-signature verification,
allowing userspace to provision IPE-specific policy-signing certificates.
Systems that do not provision the keyring retain their existing behavior.

This series is based on commit 48f936e302a9 ("ipe: update the project and
test suite links") from ipe/next. The BPF, dm-verity, and fs-verity
well-known key IDs are now in mainline [1]; KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING follows
these IDs at -12. The series should be rebased once that work is available
in ipe/next.

IPE currently checks the keyring's entry count directly. A separate
keys RFC proposes keyring_is_empty() to encapsulate this check [2].
This series does not depend on that RFC; it should use the helper if
available in the submission base.

Testing:
- Built x86_64 kernels with GCC 15.2.0 and Clang/LLD 21.1.8.
- Passed all 33 in-tree IPE parser KUnit cases under QEMU/KVM.
- Passed all 2,364 IPE CI cases under QEMU/KVM, including eight new
  .ipe keyring cases [3]. The CI changes are in draft PR [4].

[1] https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=62c457528529
[2] https://lore.kernel.org/r/user4%40example.test
[3] The CI run used a local compatibility adjustment to locate
    usr/gen_init_cpio on this kernel base.
[4] https://github.com/Integrity-Policy-Enforcement/ci/pull/4

Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber
---
Changes in v2:
- Drop the RFC designation.
- Replace ipe.keyring_unsealed with default-off CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING;
  leave provisioning and restriction of the enabled keyring to userspace.
- Require restrict_link_reject before using .ipe for policy verification.
- Access the keyring directly instead of through a lookup helper, and panic
  if keyring allocation fails.
- Explain the per-guest signing use case and the reason for avoiding a
  static private key in guest build artifacts.
- Retain the well-known key ID commit, but refine its commit message.
- Define the IPE acronym in kernel-parameters.txt.
- Document the userspace-provisioned threat model and kexec requirements.
- Drop the kselftest commit; instead, add tests to IPE CI's policy_signature
  batch [4].
- Link to v1: https://lore.kernel.org/r/user2%40example.test

From: Manuel Huber

Add a dedicated .ipe keyring for IPE policy signature verification.
With this, userspace can provision its own keys into the keyring,
then restrict it and activate it for IPE policy signature verification.

Gate creation of the keyring behind a new by-default disabled
CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING Kconfig option. When created, the keyring
is empty and writable. The keyring is used as a fallback after the
existing policy trust sources only when it is created, non-empty, and
restricted with restrict_link_reject.

This enables scenarios in which a trusted userspace component generates
an IPE policy, and creates an ephemeral policy-signing key pair,
provisions its public certificate, and restricts the IPE keyring during
the early lifetime of a system. The trusted component can then sign the
IPE policy, destroy the private key, and load and activate the policy.
During that phase, the system is considered in a trusted state whereas
the system transitions into a possibly untrusted state afterwards,
running arbitrary user-provided applications. In such a scenario, the
trusted userspace component could reside on a dm-verity protected
rootfs disk, and applications would reside on additional dm-verity
protected disks. The latter disks would be dynamically attached and
their dm-verity root hashes and/or signatures not known a priori to
launching the system.

A concrete usage scenario could be Kata Containers, which enables
running Kubernetes pods in ephemeral, headless utility VMs, possibly
without systemd. The rootfs disk is static and known beforehand, but
containerd's image layers might be acquired and transported into the
VM using the erofs snapshotter and dynamic block device attachment
using dm-verity. While in that usage scenario, signing a per-guest
policy with a pre-provisioned policy-signing certificate in the
builtin, secondary, or platform keyrings would be technically possible,
it would require including its corresponding private key in the guest
build artifacts. Making it possible to use an ephemeral,
userspace-provided key avoids shipping a static policy-signing private
key with the guest rootfs.

Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber

From: Manuel Huber

The BPF, dm-verity, and fs-verity keyrings have well-known IDs which
allow userspace to directly address them. This commit follows the same
pattern for the .ipe keyring.

This provides a direct interface independent of resolving %:.ipe through
process keyrings and /proc/keys.

Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber

Not trying to muddy the water here, but I stared / thought about this
a while and wonder if I'm missing something below...

With this Kconfig approach, aren't we now saying "if you want to use IPE,
and you want to ever use this feature, you need to make sure you seal that
keyring or else someone can replace the IPE policy!"? That seems rather
easy to foobar, and means to me at most kernels (i.e. distros) won't have
this enabled which limits how easy this is to use. I know Fan wanted this
behind some Kconfig to make it controlled by build time, but does it make
sense to keep the command line option as well to really make this opt-in
for users who have it enabled at build time? Otherwise you really are gonna
have to craft a special kernel in my mind.

Likewise, but more nitpicky, I'm not sure the restrict_link_reject
requirement buys much over the chain restriction. restrict_link_reject
stops new keys being added, but pkcs7_validate_trust() walks certs
embedded in the signature, so whoever holds the private key of any cert
in .ipe can sign a new leaf, embed it, and have a policy accepted anyway
I believe. Under both restrictions that basically means "holders of an
enrolled private key and whoever they delegate to". If the concern is a
restriction like key_or_keyring:<id> pointing at a writable keyring,
that seems like a provisioner bug rather than a reason to rule out the
chain restriction. Am I missing another reason for the stricter check?
I do realize this is rather pedantic in argument and doesn't have a place
in the use case described, but I'm wondering if a future use case will
want such a thing.

Thanks,
Andrew

Reading through this scenario again, I have a question about the design.

I suspect the reason you need a signing key inside the guest rootfs is
that you are running the snapshotter inside the VM. Have you
considered generating the snapshots on the VM host, signing the policy
there, and passing it into the guest?

The workflow would be:

1. The host generates an ephemeral signing key pair for the VM and
injects the public certificate into the guest's platform keyring via
firmware.
2. The host prepares the image snapshots, computes their dm-verity
root hashes, and signs the resulting IPE policy which allows execution
by dm-verity root hash with the ephemeral private key.
3. The host attaches the snapshot block devices and passes the signed
policy into the guest, where the guest simply loads and activates it
against .platform.

That way no private key ever needs to live in the guest, and it
confines the TCB to the VM host. Would this approach work for your
setup?

Fan

On Wed, Nov 04, 2026 at 12:14:57PM -0800, Fan Wu wrote:
> That way no private key ever needs to live in the guest, and it
> confines the TCB to the VM host. Would this approach work for
> your setup?

My main angle is confidential Kata containers [1], a usage scenario in which (Kubernetes) workload containers run in trusted, confidential VMs on untrusted hosts. This scenario involves hardware TEEs, attestation, and fine-grained policing of host-side inputs. Without getting into too many details, having an untrusted host bake trust anchors into the guest on the fly would undermine the threat model. The proposed IPE keyring gives the trusted guest the ability to construct and sign the IPE policy independently. Also note, outside of the confidential scenario for Kata containers, various Kata containers flavors are very opinionated on the guest boot flow, so I cannot rely on UEFI being present. Having a self-contained mechanism independent of firmware certificate provisioning would therefore be highly preferrable.

[1] https://confidentialcontainers.org/docs/architecture/

+Userspace-provisioned policy trust
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+When ``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled, IPE can authenticate policy
+signatures with certificates provisioned into the ``.ipe`` keyring. This
+differs from IPE's other policy trust sources, whose roots of trust originate
+in the kernel image or firmware: the userspace component that provisions the
+``.ipe`` keyring becomes part of the trusted computing base.
+
+That component must fulfill various requirements. The component must:
+
+- run before any untrusted userspace component runs
+- be backed by code from a trusted location
+- obtain its policy inputs from trusted sources
+- complete provisioning without failures before allowing untrusted code to
+  run. This includes adding all intended certificates, applying the
+  reject-all keyring restriction, and removing the keyring permissions which
+  would allow later modification.
+- destroy the policy-signing private key after signing the policy, if it
+  generated one.
+
+The ``.ipe`` keyring authenticates policy signatures; it does not make the
+active policy immutable or otherwise change authorization for IPE's
+securityfs control interfaces.
+
+Note on Kexec: Kexec bypasses firmware and bootloader trust checks and does
+not preserve the ``.ipe`` keyring or active policy. Deployments must thus
+prevent unauthorized kexec or establish equivalent trust in the replacement
+environment, including any initramfs and command line. Controls that deny
+further kexec loading do not prevent execution of an already-loaded image,
+so any previously loaded image must satisfy the same trust requirements or
+be unloaded before those controls take effect.
+

+Provisioning the IPE policy keyring
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+The ``.ipe`` keyring allows a system to provision an IPE-specific policy
+signing certificate without embedding it in the kernel or firmware trust
+stores. It is not linked into any process keyring. Userspace addresses it
+directly with the ``KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING`` special key ID (``-12``), which does
+not grant possession of the keyring.
+
+The keyring exists when ``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled and starts
+empty and writable. If the option is disabled, using
+``KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING`` fails with ``ENOKEY``. Userspace can add a DER-encoded
+X.509 certificate and then apply a reject-all restriction::
+
+   keyctl padd asymmetric "" -12 < policy-signing-key.der
+   keyctl restrict_keyring -12
+
+Both steps are required. IPE ignores the keyring until it is nonempty and its
+restriction is the reject-all restriction installed by the second command, so
+a partially provisioned, mutable keyring is not a trust source. The
+restriction cannot be removed. More than one certificate can be enrolled by
+repeating the ``keyctl padd`` command before restricting the keyring.
+
+Restriction prevents adding keys, but it does not prevent userspace from
+removing keys or otherwise disabling the keyring. To lock it against further
+userspace modification, drop its write and setattr permissions::
+
+   keyctl setperm -12 0x08030000
+
+This retains the permissions needed for verification and inspection.
+Provisioning, restriction, and permission hardening must be completed as
+described in `Userspace-provisioned policy trust`_ before relying on ``.ipe``
+as a trust source.
+
+Once nonempty and restricted, ``.ipe`` is searched after the configured system
+trust sources. An absent, empty, or unrestricted ``.ipe`` keyring is ignored.
+

-deploy policy updates.
+done via a signature chained to a trust source in the kernel. IPE can use the
+builtin trusted keyring and, when configured, the secondary and platform
+keyrings. This matches systems where the entity that establishes the kernel or
+firmware trust store is also authorized to deploy policy updates.
+
+When ``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled, IPE also has a dedicated
+``.ipe`` keyring for deployments that establish an IPE-specific trust anchor
+from userspace. In this case, IPE uses it as a fallback after the configured
+system keyrings, but only when it is nonempty and has a reject-all
+restriction. This model makes the userspace component that provisions and
+restricts ``.ipe`` part of the trusted computing base, for instance a
+component running in early stages of the lifecycle of a system. The
+threat model and provisioning requirements are documented in
+:doc:`/admin-guide/LSM/ipe`.
